Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 3.pdf ---
IPG Job Manager
So the thing is, right now our grid users rely on Globus GRAM 
to run their jobs on remote machines across IPG, and honestly 
it just doesn't cut it anymore. People keep asking for things 
like being able to stage several sets of files at once, run 
more than one executable as part of the same submission, and 
actually look back at what happened with a job after the fact 
— none of that is really there today. We keep hearing 
complaints that there's no good history of executions, so when 
something goes wrong nobody can tell what happened or why. 
 
What I'm picturing is a Job Manager that lets users move and 
copy files between systems and kick off applications on 
whatever machine they're authorized to use, and they should be 
able to do this either through an API or from the command 
line, whichever fits their workflow. The core idea is a job 
made up of a main sequence of steps — file operations and 
execution operations chained together reliably — and then, if 
they want, an optional cleanup part that fires afterwards to 
delete temp files and directories whether the job succeeded or 
blew up halfway through. If something fails partway through 
the main sequence, I'd expect the system to stop, run the 
cleanup tied to whatever failed plus the cleanup for 
everything that already ran, going backwards, so we don't 
leave junk scattered across machines. 
 
It also needs to play nice with how the grid already handles 
security — there's a proxy/credential thing tied into the Grid 
Security Infrastructure that has to be respected, and only 
authorized users should ever be able to touch the systems on 
the list the Job Manager manages. And whatever we build, it 
has to keep some kind of resource list so people can only 
submit to machines that are actually registered, not just 
anywhere. 
 
On the people side, we've basically got two kinds of usage. 
Regular users will connect through the client side — find a 
server, submit a job, check on it, cancel it, look up old 
runs, that sort of thing. Then there's the admin side: someone 
has to install and keep the server itself running, someone 
manages the actual hardware and OS underneath it (might be the 
same person, might not), and there's also whoever takes care 
of the software repository server. Worth keeping in mind these 
admin folks need their own way to manage who has access, 
manage that resource list, browse jobs, and have some kind of 
log of what admin actions were taken. 
 
A couple of things I want to be upfront about not worrying 
about right now. Running one application split across two 
machines at the same time with them talking to each other — 
co-scheduling, that kind of multi-machine parallel execution — 
that's interesting but not something we need for this round. 
Same with building out a full workflow/DAG language with a GUI 
to draw out job flows, staging files in parallel instead of 
one at a time, juggling file permissions across different OS 
types when staging, or any kind of file caching to speed 
things up — all of that can wait, it's not critical for what 
we need delivered now. Also heads up, this version won't be a 
drop-in replacement for whatever the old Job Manager did 
before, so we'll need to help existing users transition rather 
than assume their old scripts just keep working. 
 
One more practical thing: whatever we ship needs to actually 
tell people when something breaks — a real error name, a 
message, and ideally the reason behind it, plus a way to log 
errors to a file users can point to themselves. And it should 
have some sense of timeouts so things don't just hang forever 
waiting on a response. 
 
One more thing since this is federal software built for NASA's 
IPG program, the whole thing has to meet Section 508 
accessibility requirements, not just some corner of it, so 
that's not something we can skip just because most of our 
users are pretty technical.

Sistema: IPG Job Manager

Resumo executivo: The IPG Job Manager is a job orchestration system for NASA's Information Power Grid that enables authorized grid users to stage multiple file sets, execute multiple applications sequentially on registered remote resources, monitor and cancel jobs, inspect execution history, and perform deterministic cleanup after success or failure. It replaces current reliance on Globus GRAM for these workflows while providing API and command-line access, GSI-compatible security, administrative controls, structured error reporting, timeout handling, and Section 508 accessibility.

Escopo: The IPG Job Manager coordinates sequential file and application operations on authorized, registered IPG resources through an API and command-line client.
  Em escopo: Server discovery and client connection
  Em escopo: Job submission through API and command-line interfaces
  Em escopo: Sequential staging of multiple file sets
  Em escopo: Sequential execution of multiple applications
  Em escopo: Optional cleanup after successful or failed execution
  Em escopo: Job status monitoring, cancellation, and execution history
  Em escopo: GSI proxy credential authentication and resource authorization
  Em escopo: Managed resource registry
  Em escopo: Administrative access, resource, job, and audit management
  Em escopo: Structured error reporting, user-configurable error logging, and timeouts
  Em escopo: Section 508 accessibility across all user-facing capabilities
  Em escopo: [INFERRED] Transition guidance for users of legacy Job Manager scripts
  Fora de escopo: Co-scheduling and parallel execution of one application across multiple machines — deferred to a future release
  Fora de escopo: Full workflow or DAG definition language — not required for this release
  Fora de escopo: Graphical workflow design interface — not required for this release
  Fora de escopo: Parallel file staging — staging is sequential in this release
  Fora de escopo: Cross-operating-system file permission translation — deferred
  Fora de escopo: File caching — deferred
  Fora de escopo: Backward-compatible replacement of legacy Job Manager scripts — this release is not a drop-in replacement
  Premissa: PA-01: IPG resources expose the remote services required for file transfer and application execution.
  Premissa: PA-02: Grid users obtain valid proxy credentials through the existing Grid Security Infrastructure.
  Premissa: PA-03: Resource administrators provide valid connection and authorization information for registered resources.
  Premissa: PA-04: [INFERRED] Server and client hosts provide persistent storage for job history, audit records, and error logs.
  Restrição: REST-01 (Technological): Authentication and credential handling must integrate with the existing Grid Security Infrastructure.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Security): Jobs may target only resources registered in the Job Manager resource list and authorized for the submitting user.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Execution): Main-sequence operations and file-staging operations must execute sequentially.
  Restrição: REST-04 (Compatibility): The release is not required to preserve compatibility with legacy Job Manager scripts.
  Restrição: REST-05 (Regulatory): All user-facing functionality must comply with applicable Section 508 accessibility requirements.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - IPG grid user (Primary user): Discover a server, submit jobs, stage files, execute applications, monitor and cancel jobs, inspect history, and diagnose failures.
  STK-02 - Job Manager server administrator (Primary user): Install and operate the server, manage access and resources, browse jobs, and audit administrative actions.
  STK-03 - Managed resource administrator (Secondary user): Maintain the hardware and operating system of registered execution resources and coordinate their availability.
  STK-04 - Software repository administrator (External stakeholder): Maintain the repository from which Job Manager software packages are distributed.
  STK-05 - NASA IPG program and accessibility compliance authority (External stakeholder): Ensure that the federal software supports IPG objectives and satisfies Section 508.
  STK-06 - Grid Security Infrastructure (External stakeholder): Provide proxy credentials and identity information used for authentication and authorization.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Authorized grid access: Only identities possessing valid grid credentials and explicit authorization may access managed resources.
  RN-002 - Registered resource targeting: Jobs may target only resources included in the approved IPG managed-resource list.
  RN-003 - Ordered main sequence: The operations in a job's main sequence are performed one at a time in their declared order.
  RN-004 - Failure interruption: A failure in a main-sequence operation prevents all subsequent main-sequence operations from being performed.
  RN-005 - Reverse failure cleanup: After a main-sequence failure, cleanup associated with the failed operation and previously completed operations is performed in reverse execution order.
  RN-006 - Outcome-independent cleanup: Defined cleanup operations are performed after the main sequence regardless of whether the sequence succeeds or fails.
  RN-007 - Administrative accountability: Each access-management or resource-management action must be attributable to an administrator and execution time.
  RN-008 - Execution traceability: Job executions must retain sufficient historical information to determine what occurred and why a failure occurred.
  RN-009 - Single-resource execution: Each application execution operation targets one managed resource.
  RN-010 - Sequential file staging: File-staging operations are performed one at a time rather than concurrently.

Requisitos funcionais:
  RF-001 - Discover Job Manager server: The system shall return available Job Manager server connection information to an authorized client. [Must have]
  RF-002 - Submit job through API: The system shall accept a valid job submission through a programmatic API. [Must have]
  RF-003 - Submit job through command line: The system shall accept a valid job submission through a command-line client. [Must have]
  RF-004 - Define multiple file sets: The system shall accept multiple file-operation sets within one job definition. [Must have]
  RF-005 - Define multiple application executions: The system shall accept multiple single-resource application execution operations within one job definition. [Must have]
  RF-006 - Copy files: The system shall copy specified files between authorized systems. [Must have]
  RF-007 - Move files: The system shall move specified files between authorized systems. [Must have]
  RF-008 - Execute ordered main sequence: The system shall execute main-sequence operations one at a time in their declared order. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Define cleanup sequence: The system shall accept an optional cleanup sequence containing temporary file or directory deletion operations. [Must have]
  RF-010 - Cleanup after success: The system shall execute the defined cleanup sequence after successful completion of the main sequence. [Must have]
  RF-011 - Stop main sequence after failure: The system shall stop the main sequence when an operation fails. [Must have]
  RF-012 - Cleanup after failure: The system shall execute applicable cleanup operations in reverse execution order after a main-sequence failure. [Must have]
  RF-013 - Validate GSI credential: The system shall authenticate a client by validating its Grid Security Infrastructure proxy credential. [Must have]
  RF-014 - Authorize resource access: The system shall verify that the authenticated user is authorized for the requested target resource. [Must have]
  RF-015 - Restrict targets to registered resources: The system shall reject a job that targets a resource absent from the managed-resource list. [Must have]
  RF-016 - Check job status: The system shall return the current status of a job accessible to the requesting user. [Must have]
  RF-017 - Cancel job: The system shall accept a cancellation request for a cancellable job accessible to the requesting user. [Must have]
  RF-018 - List execution history: The system shall list historical job executions accessible to the requesting user. [Must have]
  RF-019 - Retrieve execution record: The system shall return the recorded status, timestamps, operation outcomes, and failure details for a selected job execution. [Must have]
  RF-020 - Manage user access: The system shall allow an authorized administrator to grant or revoke user access. [Must have]
  RF-021 - Manage resource list: The system shall allow an authorized administrator to add, update, or remove managed-resource records. [Must have]
  RF-022 - Browse jobs administratively: The system shall allow an authorized administrator to browse jobs managed by the server. [Must have]
  RF-023 - Record administrative actions: The system shall record each access-management and resource-management action in an administrative audit log. [Must have]
  RF-024 - Report structured errors: The system shall report a defined error name, descriptive message, and available causal reason for each failed operation. [Must have]
  RF-025 - Write user error log: The system shall write error records to a file location specified by the user. [Must have]
  RF-026 - Enforce operation timeout: The system shall terminate waiting for a remote response when the configured operation timeout expires. [Must have]
  RF-027 - Monitor server operation: The system shall allow an authorized administrator to retrieve the operational status of the Job Manager server. [Should have]

Requisitos não funcionais:
  RNF-001 (Interaction Capability) - The system shall pass 100% of the applicable Section 508 acceptance tests for every user-facing API, command-line, documentation, and administrative capability. | Métrica: 100% of applicable Section 508 test cases passed with zero critical accessibility defects.
  RNF-002 (Security) - The system shall deny 100% of protected requests that lack a valid GSI proxy credential. | Métrica: 100% denial across the authentication security test suite; zero unauthorized protected operations.
  RNF-003 (Security) - The system shall deny 100% of attempts to operate on resources for which the authenticated user lacks authorization. | Métrica: 100% of unauthorized resource-access attempts rejected and logged.
  RNF-004 (Performance Efficiency) - The system shall return job status and history queries within [TBD] 2 seconds at the 95th percentile under 100 concurrent clients. | Métrica: 95th-percentile response time at or below [TBD] 2 seconds with 100 concurrent clients.

  RNF-006 (Reliability) - The system shall retain 100% of completed job execution records for at least [TBD] 365 days. | Métrica: No missing execution records during retention validation; minimum retention period of [TBD] 365 days.
  RNF-007 (Security) - The system shall record administrator identity, action, target, outcome, and timestamp for 100% of audited administrative operations. | Métrica: 100% of tested administrative operations produce complete audit records.
  RNF-008 (Reliability) - The system shall provide [TBD] 99.5% monthly server availability excluding approved maintenance windows. | Métrica: Monthly availability greater than or equal to [TBD] 99.5%.

Casos de uso:
  UC-001 - Discover a Job Manager server | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The actor requests Job Manager server discovery.
    2. The system validates the actor's credential.
    3. The system identifies an available server.
    4. The system returns the server connection information.
  UC-002 - Submit a job | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The actor sends a job definition through the API.
    2. The system validates the job structure.
    3. The system validates the target resource and authorization.
    4. The system creates the job record.
    5. The system returns the job identifier and accepted status.
  UC-003 - Execute a sequential job | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The system selects the first main-sequence operation.
    2. The system performs the operation.
    3. The system records the operation outcome.
    4. The system selects the next operation.
    5. Steps 2 through 4 repeat until all main operations complete.
    6. The system marks the main sequence as successful.
  UC-004 - Perform job cleanup | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The system identifies the applicable cleanup operations.
    2. The system executes each cleanup operation in the required order.
    3. The system records each cleanup outcome.
    4. The system finalizes the job status.
  UC-005 - Authenticate and authorize user | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The actor sends a protected request with a proxy credential.
    2. The system validates the credential.
    3. The system identifies the actor.
    4. The system verifies authorization for the requested resource.
    5. The system permits the requested operation.
  UC-006 - Check job status | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The actor requests status using a job identifier.
    2. The system verifies access to the job.
    3. The system retrieves the current status.
    4. The system returns the status to the actor.
  UC-007 - Cancel a job | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The actor requests cancellation using a job identifier.
    2. The system verifies job access and state.
    3. The system stops further main-sequence processing.
    4. The system performs applicable cleanup.
    5. The system records and returns cancelled status.
  UC-008 - Inspect job history | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The actor requests historical executions.
    2. The system returns jobs accessible to the actor.
    3. The actor selects an execution.
    4. The system returns timestamps, operation outcomes, status, and failure details.
  UC-009 - Manage user access | Ator: Job Manager server administrator
    1. The actor selects a user identity.
    2. The actor grants or revokes access.
    3. The system validates the requested change.
    4. The system applies the change.
    5. The system records the administrative action.
  UC-010 - Manage registered resources | Ator: Job Manager server administrator
    1. The actor requests to add, update, or remove a resource.
    2. The system validates the resource record.
    3. The system updates the managed-resource list.
    4. The system records the administrative action.
    5. The system confirms the resulting resource state.
  UC-011 - Browse managed jobs | Ator: Job Manager server administrator
    1. The actor requests jobs managed by the server.
    2. The system verifies administrative privileges.
    3. The system retrieves matching jobs.
    4. The system returns job summaries.
    5. The actor may select a job to view its execution record.
  UC-012 - Write user error log | Ator: IPG grid user
    1. The actor configures an error-log file location.
    2. A job operation fails.
    3. The system creates a structured error record.
    4. The system writes the record to the configured file.
    5. The system reports the error to the actor.

Critérios de aceite:
  CA-001 - Dado a client with a valid GSI credential and at least one available server, quando the client requests server discovery, então the system returns at least one server identifier and connection endpoint.
  CA-002 - Dado a valid API job definition targeting an authorized registered resource, quando the definition is submitted, então the system returns a unique job identifier and status 'Accepted'.
  CA-003 - Dado a valid job definition supplied to the command-line client, quando the user executes the submission command, então the command exits with code 0 and displays a unique job identifier.
  CA-004 - Dado a job definition containing three valid file-operation sets, quando the job is validated, então all three file-operation sets are accepted in the declared job.
  CA-005 - Dado a job definition containing three application execution operations, quando the job is validated, então all three execution operations are accepted with one target resource per operation.
  CA-006 - Dado an authorized source file and destination path, quando a copy operation executes, então the destination contains a byte-identical file and the source remains present.
  CA-007 - Dado an authorized source file and destination path, quando a move operation executes, então the destination contains a byte-identical file and the source path no longer contains the file.
  CA-008 - Dado a job containing operations A, B, and C, quando the main sequence executes successfully, então the execution record shows A completed before B started and B completed before C started.
  CA-009 - Dado a job definition containing cleanup deletion operations, quando the job is validated, então the cleanup sequence is accepted and stored with the job definition.
  CA-010 - Dado a successful main sequence with a temporary file covered by cleanup, quando the main sequence completes, então the temporary file is deleted and the cleanup operation is recorded as 'Succeeded'.
  CA-011 - Dado a main sequence in which operation B fails before operation C, quando operation B reports failure, então operation C is not started and the main sequence status becomes 'Failed'.
  CA-012 - Dado operations A and B completed before operation C failed, quando failure cleanup begins, então cleanup executes for C, then B, then A, with that order recorded in history.
  CA-013 - Dado a request containing a valid unexpired GSI proxy credential, quando the request reaches a protected endpoint, então the system authenticates the represented identity and continues authorization processing.
  CA-014 - Dado an authenticated user without authorization for resource R, quando the user submits an operation targeting R, então the operation is rejected with status 'AccessDenied' and no remote action is initiated.
  CA-015 - Dado a job targeting a resource absent from the managed-resource list, quando the job is submitted, então the submission is rejected with status 'ResourceNotRegistered'.
  CA-016 - Dado an accessible running job, quando the user requests its status, então the response contains the job identifier and status 'Running'.
  CA-017 - Dado an accessible job in a cancellable state, quando the user requests cancellation, então the job reaches status 'Cancelled' and no subsequent main operation starts.
  CA-018 - Dado a user with two completed accessible jobs, quando the user requests execution history, então the result contains both job identifiers, final statuses, and submission timestamps.
  CA-019 - Dado a selected failed job containing three recorded operations, quando the user requests its execution record, então the response contains all three operation outcomes, timestamps, final status, error name, message, and available reason.
  CA-020 - Dado an administrator and an existing user identity, quando the administrator revokes that user's access, então subsequent protected requests by that user are denied and the change is recorded.
  CA-021 - Dado an administrator and a valid unregistered resource record, quando the administrator adds the resource, então the resource appears exactly once in the managed-resource list.
  CA-022 - Dado an authorized administrator and jobs managed by the server, quando the administrator requests the job list, então the system returns the managed jobs with identifiers, owners, submission times, and statuses.
  CA-023 - Dado an administrator updating a resource record, quando the update completes, então one audit record is created containing administrator identity, action, target, outcome, and timestamp.
  CA-024 - Dado a job operation that fails for a known cause, quando the failure is reported, então the error contains a non-empty defined name, message, and causal reason.
  CA-025 - Dado a writable file location configured by the user, quando a job error occurs, então the error record is appended to that file within [TBD] 5 seconds.
  CA-026 - Dado a remote service that provides no response, quando the configured timeout of [TBD] 60 seconds expires, então the wait terminates within 1 additional second and reports status 'TimedOut'.
  CA-027 - Dado an authorized administrator and an operating server, quando the administrator requests server status, então the system returns status 'Operational' and a response timestamp within [TBD] 2 seconds.

Glossário:
  IPG: NASA's Information Power Grid environment containing distributed computing resources.
  Job: A submitted unit of work containing an ordered main sequence and an optional cleanup sequence.
  Main sequence: The ordered sequence of file and application execution operations that implements the primary job objective.
  Cleanup sequence: Optional operations that remove temporary files or directories after the main sequence terminates.
  File staging: Copying or moving input, output, or temporary files between systems involved in a job.
  Managed resource: A remote machine registered in the Job Manager resource list and eligible to receive authorized operations.
  GSI: Grid Security Infrastructure used to provide grid identities and proxy credentials.
  Proxy credential: A delegated, time-limited grid credential used to authenticate a user or client.
  Globus GRAM: The existing grid job submission mechanism currently used by IPG users.
  Co-scheduling: Coordinated execution of one parallel workload across multiple machines, excluded from this release.
  DAG: Directed Acyclic Graph used to represent general workflow dependencies, excluded from this release.
  Section 508: United States federal accessibility requirements applicable to the system's user-facing capabilities.

Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.
1.2 Como os Artefatos se Interconectam
Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.

Expected challenges
The presence of an existing system leads to common challenges that both enhancement and 
replacement projects will face, including the following:
■ The changes made could degrade the performance to which users are accustomed.
■ Little or no requirements documentation might be available for the existing system.
■ Users who are familiar with how the system works today might not like the changes they are 
about to encounter.
■ You might unknowingly break or omit functionality that is vital to some stakeholder group.
■ Stakeholders might take this opportunity to request new functionality that seems like a good 
idea but isn’t really needed to meet the business objectives.
Even if there is existing documentation, it might not prove useful. For enhancement projects, 
the documentation might not be up to date. If the documentation doesn’t match the existing 
application’s reality, it is of limited use. For replacement systems, you also need to be wary of carrying 
forward all of the requirements, because some of the old functionality probably should not be 
migrated.
One of the major issues in replacement projects is validating that the reasons for the replacement 
are sound. There need to be justifiable business objectives for the change. When existing systems 
are being completely replaced, organizational processes might also have to change, which makes it 
harder for people to accept a new system. The change in business processes, change in the software 
system, and learning curve of a new system can disrupt current operations.

É Stakeholder ou Ator?
Stakeholder = quem tem interesse no sistema (pode não usá-lo diretamente).
Ator (Caso de Uso) = quem INTERAGE diretamente com o sistema.
Todo Ator é Stakeholder; nem todo Stakeholder é Ator.
É Premissa ou Restrição?
Premissa = fato ASSUMIDO como verdadeiro sem confirmação formal. Pode mudar.
Restrição = limite IMPOSTO que não pode ser negociado (lei, orçamento, prazo, tech).
É escopo IN ou OUT?
IN = funcionalidade que o SISTEMA DO PROJETO vai implementar.
OUT = funcionalidade que fica em outro sistema ou versão futura.
Regra prática: se está em outro sistema já existente → OUT.PARTE 4 — Armadilhas Comuns na Extração Automática

4.1 Palavras Proibidas em Requisitos
As palavras abaixo indicam requisitos ambíguos, subjetivos ou não verificáveis. Quando 
encontradas, o requisito deve ser reescrito com métricas objetivas.
• rápido / veloz / ágil: Substituir por: 'tempo de resposta inferior a X ms/s'
• fácil / simples / intuitivo: Substituir por: métrica de usabilidade (ex.: task completion em < N min)
• amigável / bonito / moderno: Atributo subjetivo — vai para diretrizes de UI, não para RF/RNF
• eficiente: Substituir por: consumo de CPU < X%, throughput > Y req/s
• seguro: Substituir por: característica específica da ISO 25010 Security com métrica
• geralmente / normalmente: Indica exceções não documentadas — especificar todas as condições
• etc. / e assim por diante: Indica incompletude — listar todos os itens explicitamente

to run their jobs on remote machines across IPG, and honestly 
it just doesn't cut it anymore. People keep asking for things

execution operations chained together reliably — and then, if

3.7 Protótipos na Engenharia de Requisitos (L1)
Na ER, os protótipos são um meio de especificar os requisitos através do exemplo e de 
validar os requisitos. Em particular, os protótipos podem ser usados se os stakeholders não 
quiserem escrever e revisar produtos de trabalho baseados em linguagem natural ou em

Os protótipos exploratórios [LiSZ1994] são usados para criar um entendimento comum,

descartados após o uso.
▪ Wireframes são protótipos de baixa fidelidade construídos com materiais simples ou 
ferramentas de esboço que servem principalmente para discutir e validar ideias de 
design e conceitos de interface com o usuário.

If you’re replacing an old system, you have an opportunity to document 
the requirements for the new one and to keep the requirements up to date with what you learn 
throughout the project. Try to leave the requirements in better shape than you found them.
Which requirements should you specify?
It’s not always worth taking the time to generate a complete set of requirements for an entire 
production system. Many options lie between the two extremes of continuing forever with no 
requirements documentation and reconstructing a perfect requirements set. Knowing why you’d like 
to have written requirements available lets you judge whether the cost of rebuilding all—or even 
part—of the specification is a sound investment.

Rarely do you need to document the entire existing system. Focus detailed requirements efforts 
on the changes needed to meet the business objectives. If you’re replacing a system, start by 
documenting the areas prioritized as most important to achieve the business objectives or those that 
pose the highest implementation risk. Any new requirements identified during the gap analysis will 
need to be specified at the same level of precision and using the same techniques as you would for a 
new system.
Level of detail
One of the biggest challenges is determining the appropriate level of detail at which to document 
requirements gleaned from the existing system. For enhancements, defining requirements for the 
new functionality alone might be sufficient. However, you will usually benefit from documenting all of 
the functionality that closely relates to the enhancement, to ensure that the change fits in seamlessly 
(region B in Figure 21-2). You might want to create business processes, user requirements, and/or 
functional requirements for those related areas. For example, let’s say you are adding a discount code 
feature to an existing shopping cart function, but you don’t have any documented requirements for 
the shopping cart. You might be tempted to write just a single user story: “As a customer, I need to be 
able to enter a discount code so I can get the cheapest price for the product.” However, this user story 
alone lacks context, so consider capturing other user stories about shopping cart operations. That 
information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.
I worked with one team that was just beginning to develop the requirements for version 2 of 
a major product with embedded software. They hadn’t done a good job on the requirements for 
version 1, which was currently being implemented. The lead BA wondered, “Is it worth going back 
to improve the SRS for version 1?” The company anticipated that this product line would be a major 
revenue generator for at least 10 years. They also planned to reuse some of the core requirements 
in several spin-off products. In this case, it made sense to improve the requirements documentation 
for version 1 because it was the foundation for all subsequent development work in this product line.

CHAPTER 21
Enhancement and replacement 
projects
Most of this book describes requirements development as though you are beginning a new software 
or system development project, sometimes called a green-field project. However, many organizations 
devote much of their effort to enhancing or replacing existing information systems or building 
new releases of established commercial products. Most of the practices described in this book are 
appropriate for enhancement and replacement projects. This chapter provides specific suggestions as 
to which practices are most relevant and how to use them.
An enhancement project is one in which new capabilities are added to an existing system. 
Enhancement projects might also involve correcting defects, adding new reports, and modifying 
functionality to comply with revised business rules or needs.
A replacement (or reengineering) project replaces an existing application with a new custom-built 
system, a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) system, or a hybrid of those. Replacement projects are 
most commonly implemented to improve performance, cut costs (such as maintenance costs or 
license fees), take advantage of modern technologies, or meet regulatory requirements. If your 
replacement project will involve a COTS solution, the guidance presented in Chapter 22, “Packaged 
solution projects,” will also be helpful.
Replacement and enhancement projects face some particular requirements issues. The original 
developers who held all the critical information in their heads might be long gone. It’s tempting to 
claim that a small enhancement doesn’t warrant writing any requirements. Developers might believe 
that they don’t need detailed requirements if they are replacing an existing system’s functionality. 
The approaches described in this chapter can help you to deal with the challenges of enhancing or 
replacing an existing system to improve its ability to meet the organization’s current business needs.
The case of the missing spec
The requirements specification for the next release of a mature system often says, essentially, 
“The new system should do everything the old system does, except add these new features 
and fix those bugs.” A business analyst once received just such a specification for version 5 of 
a major product. To find out exactly what the current release did, she looked at the SRS for 
version 4. Unfortunately, it also said, in essence, “Version 4 should do everything that version 3 
does, except add these new features and fix those bugs.” She followed the trail back, but every

If developers build exactly what 
customers initially request, they’ll probably have to build it again because customers often don’t 
know what they really need. In addition, the BAs might not be talking to the right people or asking 
the right questions.
The features that users present as their “wants” don’t necessarily equate to the functionality they 
need to perform their tasks with the new product. To gain a more accurate view of user needs, the 
business analyst must collect a wide range of user input, analyze and clarify it, and specify just what 
needs to be built to let users do their jobs. The BA has the lead responsibility for recording the new 
system’s necessary capabilities and properties and for communicating that information to other 
stakeholders. This is an iterative process that takes time. If you don’t invest the time to achieve this 
shared understanding—this common vision of the intended product—the certain outcomes are 
rework, missed deadlines, cost overruns, and customer dissatisfaction.
User classes
People often talk about “the user” for a software system as though all users belong to a monolithic 
group with similar characteristics and needs. In reality, most products of any size appeal to a diversity 
of users with different expectations and goals. Rather than thinking of “the user” in singular, spend 
some time identifying the multiple user classes and their roles and privileges for your product.
Classifying users
Chapter 2 described many of the types of stakeholders that a project might have. As shown in 
Figure 6-1, a user class is a subset of the product’s users, which is a subset of the product’s customers, 
which is a subset of its stakeholders. An individual can belong to multiple user classes. For example, 
an application’s administrator might also interact with it as an ordinary user at times. A product’s 
users might differ—among other ways—in the following respects, and you can group users into a 
number of distinct user classes based on these sorts of differences:
■ Their access privilege or security levels (such as ordinary user, guest user, administrator)
■ The tasks they perform during their business operations
■ The features they use
■ The frequency with which they use the product
■ Their application domain experience and computer systems expertise
■ The platforms they will be using (desktop PCs, laptop PCs, tablets, smartphones, specialized 
devices)CHAPTER 6 Finding the voice of the user 103
■ Their native language
■ Whether they will interact with the system directly or indirectly
FIGURE 6-1 A hierarchy of stakeholders, customers, users, and user classes.
It’s tempting to group users into classes based on their geographical location or the kind of 
company they work in. One company that creates software used in the banking industry initially 
considered distinguishing users based on whether they worked in a large commercial bank, a small 
commercial bank, a savings and loan institution, or a credit union. These distinctions really represent 
different market segments, though, not different user classes.
A better way to identify user classes is to think about the tasks that various users will perform with 
the system. All of those types of financial institutions will have tellers, employees who process loan 
applications, business bankers, and so forth. The individuals who perform such activities—whether 
they are job titles or simply roles—will have similar functional needs for the system across all of the 
financial institutions. Tellers all have to do more or less the same things, business bankers do more or 
less the same things, and so on. More logical user class names for a banking system therefore might 
include teller, loan officer, business banker, and branch manager. You might discover additional user 
classes by thinking of possible use cases, user stories, and process flows and who might perform them.

Trap Don’t let stakeholders get away with saying “I have it today, so I need it in the new 
system” as a default method of justifying requirements.
Mind the gap
A gap analysis is a comparison of functionality between an existing system and a desired new system. 
A gap analysis can be expressed in different ways, including use cases, user stories, or features. When 
enhancing an existing system, perform a gap analysis to make sure you understand why it isn’t 
currently meeting your business objectives.
Gap analysis for a replacement project entails understanding existing functionality and discovering 
the desired new functionality (see Figure 21-1). Identify user requirements for the existing system that 
stakeholders want to have re-implemented in the new system. Also, elicit new user requirements that 
the existing system does not address. Consider any change requests that were never implemented CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 397
in the existing system. Prioritize the existing user requirements and the new ones together. Prioritize 
closing the gaps using business objectives as described in the previous section or the other 
prioritization techniques presented in Chapter 16, “First things first: Setting requirement priorities.”
FIGURE 21-1 When you are replacing an existing system, some requirements will be implemented unchanged, 
some will be modified, some will be discarded, and some new requirements might be added.
Maintaining performance levels
Existing systems set user expectations for performance and throughput. Stakeholders almost 
always have key performance indicators (KPIs) for existing processes that they will want to maintain 
in the new system. A key performance indicator model (KPIM) can help you identify and specify 
these metrics for their corresponding business processes (Beatty and Chen 2012). The KPIM helps 
stakeholders see that even if the new system will be different, their business outcomes will be at least 
as good as before.
Unless you explicitly plan to maintain them, performance levels can be compromised as systems 
are enhanced. Stuffing new functionality into an existing system might slow it down. One data 
synchronization tool had a requirement to update a master data set from the day’s transactions. 
It needed to run every 24 hours. In the initial release of the tool, the synchronization started at 
midnight and took about one hour to execute. After some enhancements to include additional 
attributes, merging, and synchronicity checks, the synchronization took 20 hours to execute. This was 
a problem, because users expected to have fully synchronized data from the night before available 
when they started their workday at 8:00 A.M. The maximum time to complete the synchronization 
was never explicitly specified, but the stakeholders assumed it could be done overnight in less than 
eight hours.
For replacement systems, prioritize the KPIs that are most important to maintain. Look for the 
business processes that trace to the most important KPIs and the requirements that enable those 
business processes; these are the requirements to implement first. For instance, if you’re replacing a 
loan application system in which loan processors can enter 10 loans per day, it might be important 
to maintain at least that same throughput in the new system. The functionality that allows loan 
processers to enter loans should be some of the earliest implemented in the new system, so the loan 
processors can maintain their productivity.

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The client possesses a valid GSI proxy credential.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The client receives server connection information.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No connection information is returned and a structured error is reported.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor requests Job Manager server discovery.
2. The system validates the actor's credential.
3. The system identifies an available server.
4. The system returns the server connection information.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. Multiple servers are available → the system returns the eligible server list.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. The credential is invalid → the system denies the request and reports an authentication error (ref. RN-001, RF-013).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authenticated and the job targets a registered resource.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A job record is created with a unique identifier and accepted status.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No executable job is created and validation errors are returned.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor sends a job definition through the API.
2. The system validates the job structure.
3. The system validates the target resource and authorization.
4. The system creates the job record.
5. The system returns the job identifier and accepted status.
fluxos_alternativos: 1a. The actor submits through the command-line client → the system applies the same validation and submission process (ref. RF-003).
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The resource is unregistered or unauthorized → the system rejects the submission and reports the reason (ref. RN-001, RN-002, RF-014, RF-015).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: A valid job has been accepted and its target resources are available.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: All main operations have completed in order and the job reaches completed status.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: Execution stops at the failed operation and the job reaches failed status after cleanup processing.
fluxo_principal: 1. The system selects the first main-sequence operation.
2. The system performs the operation.
3. The system records the operation outcome.
4. The system selects the next operation.
5. Steps 2 through 4 repeat until all main operations complete.
6. The system marks the main sequence as successful.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The operation is a file operation → the system copies or moves the specified files before continuing.
2b. The operation is an application execution → the system starts the application on its single target resource.
fluxos_excecao: 2c. An operation fails → the system stops the main sequence and initiates reverse cleanup (ref. RN-004, RN-005, RF-011, RF-012).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The job contains cleanup operations and its main sequence has terminated.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: Applicable temporary files and directories are deleted and cleanup outcomes are recorded.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: Cleanup errors are recorded without erasing the original job outcome.
fluxo_principal: 1. The system identifies the applicable cleanup operations.
2. The system executes each cleanup operation in the required order.
3. The system records each cleanup outcome.
4. The system finalizes the job status.
fluxos_alternativos: 1a. The main sequence succeeded → the system executes the defined cleanup sequence.
1b. The main sequence failed → the system executes applicable cleanup in reverse execution order.
fluxos_excecao: 2c. A cleanup deletion fails → the system records a structured cleanup error and continues with the remaining applicable cleanup operations (ref. RF-024).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor has obtained a GSI proxy credential.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The actor is authenticated and permitted to access the requested registered resource.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor sends a protected request with a proxy credential.
2. The system validates the credential.
3. The system identifies the actor.
4. The system verifies authorization for the requested resource.
5. The system permits the requested operation.
fluxos_excecao: 2a. The credential is invalid or expired → the system denies the request (ref. RN-001, RF-013).
4a. The actor lacks resource authorization → the system denies the request (ref. RN-001, RF-014).
4b. The resource is not registered → the system rejects the request (ref. RN-002, RF-015).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The requested job exists and is accessible to the actor.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The current job status is returned.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor requests status using a job identifier.
2. The system verifies access to the job.
3. The system retrieves the current status.
4. The system returns the status to the actor.
fluxos_excecao: 2a. The job is absent or inaccessible → the system returns a structured not-found or access-denied error (ref. RF-024).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The job exists, is accessible to the actor, and is in a cancellable state.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The job reaches cancelled status and applicable cleanup is processed.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The existing job state remains unchanged.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor requests cancellation using a job identifier.
2. The system verifies job access and state.
3. The system stops further main-sequence processing.
4. The system performs applicable cleanup.
5. The system records and returns cancelled status.
fluxos_excecao: 2a. The job is already terminal → the system rejects cancellation and returns the current status (ref. RF-017).

casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The actor receives accessible historical executions and selected execution details.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor requests historical executions.
2. The system returns jobs accessible to the actor.
3. The actor selects an execution.
4. The system returns timestamps, operation outcomes, status, and failure details.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. No historical executions match → the system returns an empty result set.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The selected execution is inaccessible → the system denies access and records the event (ref. RN-001, RF-019).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authenticated with access-management privileges.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The selected user's access is updated and audited.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor selects a user identity.
2. The actor grants or revokes access.
3. The system validates the requested change.
4. The system applies the change.
5. The system records the administrative action.
fluxos_excecao: 3a. The requested identity or permission is invalid → the system rejects the change and records the failed action (ref. RN-007, RF-023).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authenticated with resource-management privileges.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The resource list is updated and the change is audited.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor requests to add, update, or remove a resource.
2. The system validates the resource record.
3. The system updates the managed-resource list.
4. The system records the administrative action.
5. The system confirms the resulting resource state.
fluxos_excecao: 2a. The resource record is invalid → the system rejects the update and reports validation details (ref. RN-002, RF-021).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor is authenticated with job-browsing privileges.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The administrator receives the requested job list or details.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor requests jobs managed by the server.
2. The system verifies administrative privileges.
3. The system retrieves matching jobs.
4. The system returns job summaries.
5. The actor may select a job to view its execution record.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. No jobs match → the system returns an empty result set.
fluxos_excecao: 2a. The actor lacks privileges → the system denies access (ref. RN-001, RF-022).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The actor has specified a writable error-log file location.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The error record is appended to the specified file.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The original error remains available through the active interface and the logging failure is reported.
fluxo_principal: 1. The actor configures an error-log file location.
2. A job operation fails.
3. The system creates a structured error record.
4. The system writes the record to the configured file.
5. The system reports the error to the actor.
fluxos_excecao: 4a. The file is not writable → the system reports an error-log write failure without replacing the original operation error (ref. RF-024, RF-025).

gabarito_artefatos.observacoes: Tem RNFs explicitas e verificaveis (raro entre os 9): timeout, conformidade com Section 508, estrutura de relato de erro. em_escopo: Moving and copying files between systems
Launching applications on authorized machines, via API or command line
A job composed of a main sequence of file and execution operations, executed reliably and in order
Optional cleanup step after the main sequence, on both success and failure
Reverse-order cleanup on partial failure of the main sequence
Integration with the Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism
Resource list (registered machines) and restriction of submission to those machines
Client for regular users (find server, submit, check, cancel, look up history)
Administrative functionality (manage access, manage resource list, browse jobs, admin action log)
Structured error reporting (name, message, reason) and file-based error logging
Timeouts to prevent operations from hanging indefinitely
Compliance with Section 508 accessibility

Cross-OS file permission handling during staging

PA-02: [INFERRED] Regular users have enough technical familiarity to use the API or command line.
restricoes: REST-01 (Regulatory): As federal software built for NASA's IPG program, the whole system must meet Section 508 accessibility requirements.

stakeholders.descricao: Regular user (grid user) — connects through the client to submit, check, cancel jobs, and look up old runs.
Server installer/maintainer (admin) — installs and keeps the Job Manager server running.
Hardware/OS manager (admin) — manages the underlying hardware and operating system.
Software repository server manager (admin) — manages the software repository.

regras_de_negocio.descricao: A job consists of a main sequence of file and execution operations, executed reliably and in order.
An optional cleanup step can run after the main sequence, regardless of success or failure.
On partial failure of the main sequence, cleanup must run for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
Users can only submit jobs to machines registered in the resource list.
Only authorized users (via GSI credential) can access the systems managed by the Job Manager.
This version is not a drop-in replacement for the old Job Manager — existing users need transition support, with no guarantee that old scripts keep working.

requisitos_funcionais.descricao: The system must allow users to move/copy files between systems.
The system must allow users to launch applications on machines they are authorized to use.
The system must allow these operations to be performed via API or via command line.
The system must execute a job's main sequence of file and execution operations reliably and in order.
The system must support an optional cleanup step that runs after the main sequence, on either job success or failure.
The system must, on partial failure of the main sequence, run cleanup for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
The system must integrate with the existing Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism.
The system must maintain a resource list of registered machines.
The system must restrict job submission to machines registered in the resource list.
The system must allow regular users to find an available server.
The system must allow regular users to submit a job.
The system must allow regular users to check the status of a submitted job.
The system must allow regular users to cancel a job.
The system must allow regular users to look up old job runs.
The system must allow admins to manage user access.
The system must allow admins to manage the resource list.
The system must allow admins to browse existing jobs.
The system must maintain a log of administrative actions taken.
The system must report errors with a real error name and a message, and ideally the reason.
The system must log errors to a file that the user can consult themselves.

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: System operations must implement timeouts, so they don't hang indefinitely waiting for a response.
requisitos_nao_funcionais.metrica_aceitacao: [TBD] — scenario does not define a numeric timeout duration

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: The system must fully respect the Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism to authorize access to managed resources.
requisitos_nao_funcionais.metrica_aceitacao: 100% of accesses to managed systems validated via GSI credential

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: As federal software built for NASA's IPG program, the whole system — not just part of it — must meet Section 508 accessibility requirements.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a regular user, I want to move/copy files between systems and launch applications on authorized machines via API or command line, so that I can run my jobs in whatever way fits my workflow.
As a regular user, I want to submit a job with a main sequence and an optional cleanup step, so that temporary files are removed regardless of whether the job succeeds or fails.
As a regular user, I want to check, cancel, and look up old runs of my jobs, so that I can manage and audit my own work.
As a server installer/maintainer, I want to install and keep the server running, so that the Job Manager stays available.
As an admin, I want to manage user access and the resource list, so that only authorized users submit jobs to registered machines.
As an admin, I want to browse existing jobs and see a log of administrative actions, so that I can monitor usage and my own team's actions.
As a user, I want to receive clear error messages (name, message, reason) and have errors logged to a file, so that I can diagnose failures myself.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Submit and run job — a user submits a job (main sequence of file/execution operations), the system executes it reliably and runs cleanup afterward (success or failure), including reverse-order cleanup on partial failure.
Manage job status — a user checks, cancels, or looks up the history of a submitted job.
Manage access and resources (admin) — an admin manages user access and the list of registered machines.
Review admin log — an admin browses the log of administrative actions taken on the system.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given a job that fails partway through the main sequence, when the failure occurs, then the system runs cleanup for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
Given a user attempting to submit a job to an unregistered machine, when the submission is attempted, then the system rejects it.
Given an operation waiting for a response, when the timeout threshold is reached, then the system aborts the wait instead of hanging indefinitely.
Given any part of the system's interface, when it is evaluated for accessibility, then it complies with Section 508.
Given an error occurs during job execution, when it is reported, then the system provides a real error name, a message, and logs the error to a file accessible to the user.
